source: can you make a 1v1v1v1v1v1 first person 3d game about who can find the exit first in the arcade? In the arcade there will be rooms hinting or tricking you into finding the exit! who ever finds it last loses! The game also has multiple maps ( you can decide on what they are going to be ) and everyone has to decide which map they want to play!

answers.ask: How long should a round last - is finding the exit a minute of searching, or five?
answers.answer: Make each round a quick one-minute search so the game stays fast and replayable.

answers.ask: Does the round end when the first player is out, or does everyone keep going until only the loser is left inside?
answers.answer: Everyone keeps going after finding the exit; the round ends once only the last player is still inside, and that player loses.

scene_prompt: Create a first-person 3D arcade escape map for six players, built as a compact maze of interconnected arcade rooms. Each room contains arcade machines, corridors, doorways, and misleading routes that hint at or trick players searching for the exit; place the true exit beyond the room network. Support multiple distinct arcade map layouts for players to choose from.
blob:
### 1. Genre
The dominant genre is Party & Casual: a six-player, fast round determines who escapes the arcade maze last. Puzzle is secondary because route-finding through deceptive rooms is the challenge, but Party & Casual owns the multiplayer round framing.

### 2. Shape and preset
Use `puzzle-maze`, taken from outside Party & Casual’s usual shape set. Each selected arcade is a compact, solvable maze of freely interconnected rooms and corridors with one reachable true exit; false leads are part of the route design. Preset: none, since no Party preset remains recognisable after adopting the dedicated maze topology.

### 3. Config requirements
No additional image-config options apply. Render the requested arcade machines, doorways, corridors, misleading branches, and exit architecture as the maze’s concrete dressing without adding unrequested lobby, spectators, hazards, or pickups.

### 4. Layout requirements
Use `spawn-protected` for six evenly spaced round-start markers in a safe common entry room, screened from immediate route choices so no player receives an unfair head start. Use `trigger-scoring` once at the true exit of each map, placed across the final exit doorway to register each player’s departure order. The exit trigger is placed geometry, not rendered UI.

### 5. Layout components
Build three separate selectable arcade maze maps: a neon retro cabinet arcade, a prize-and-ticket arcade with redemption counters, and a dark futuristic cyber arcade. Each map has a compact entry room, a dense network of interconnected themed arcade rooms, branching corridors, doorways, and several visually convincing dead ends or misleading routes. Arcade cabinets, claw machines, ticket counters, signboards, and decorative lighting provide clues or distractions without obscuring doorway readability. Put one unmistakable true exit beyond the far side of each room network, visually distinct only once players reach its final approach. Each maze is enclosed by arcade walls; no exterior terrain is needed. Compose each plan with the entry room near one edge, the exit on the opposing edge, and branching circulation filling the centre.

### 6. Render order
Use `authored_plan`: a maze must be valid by construction, with every start able to reach the exit and deceptive branches never sealing the only solution.

### 7. Scale, theme, and pipeline cost
Scale is medium: each arcade is compact for a one-minute search, while the three distinct maps provide replayability. Theme is colorful first-person arcade labyrinths, from retro neon to ticket-carnival to cyber-dark. Apply `P4` because the three arcade layouts are separate selectable maps, and `P6` because each maze’s traversable exit route must be solvable and connected by construction.
